assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and demonstrated with strontium, pushed fractional frequency uncertainty and stability by orders of magnitude and opened the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. This is a measurement advance of the kind that expands what can be observed, and it is clear, original and has lasting impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first Sr lattice clock; Jun Ye carried the accuracy and many-body-coherence frontier far (Sr, 10^-18 level, JILA). The two credited names form a natural pair. Other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Gill, Hinkley/Ludlow at NIST) contributed to confirmation and could raise credit questions, but the supplied credit is adequate.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many independent labs worldwide operate lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level, and comparisons between them are routine. Timing is good because the SI second redefinition is being discussed.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would want to include a third name, e.g. an early-demonstration contributor, is not settled by the supplied credit.
I have not independently verified the latest accuracy numbers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave atom interferometry turned atoms into inertial sensors, enabling precision gravimetry, gradiometry, measurements of G and the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. This is a new measurement method with real field-opening impact and growing application in geodesy and navigation.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theoretical and Ramsey-Bordé interferometer work, Pritchard's early atom-optics and interferometer demonstrations (MIT) and Kasevich's precision gravimeter and large-scale devices are distinct contributions. Others (Chu, Ertmer, Mlynek, Keith) complicate the picture; Chu already holds a prize for laser cooling.
assessment.maturity: Mature as a laboratory technique, with strong independent replication and commercial gravimeters. Large-baseline and space-based uses remain developing, which does not undermine the core discovery.
uncertainties: Credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and the Konstanz and Paris groups is contested and the supplied trio may not be the fairest.
Relative weight of the first demonstrations versus precision-measurement development is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Single-NV-center optical detection and coherent spin control at room temperature created a platform for nanoscale magnetic, electric and temperature sensing, with consequences from quantum networking to biology. It is a measurement capability that has clearly opened a field.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated optical readout of single NV spins and coherent control; Lukin contributed nanoscale sensing, quantum registers and many-body sensing. Gruber and Hanson/Awschalom groups are also significant. The trio is plausible but Lukin's role is broader than this topic.
assessment.maturity: Mature: widely reproduced in many labs, with commercial products and sensing applications emerging. Applied impact is still developing relative to the originating demonstrations.
uncertainties: Whether Lukin's contributions or others (Awschalom, Hanson, Gruber) deserve the third place.
Applied sensing impact beyond physics is still unproven at scale.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard models with tunable parameters and single-site readout, via the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and quantum gas microscopes. This gives a controlled quantum simulator and a new way to observe many-body states.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and Cirac) supplied the proposal; Bloch and Greiner carried out the Mott-insulator experiments and quantum gas microscopy. Greiner and Bloch both led microscope work, and Cirac's role in theory competes with Zoller's. Hänsch and Esslinger are further contributors.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for the Mott transition and microscopy. Quantum simulation of open problems such as the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram is still in progress, so some of the stated promise is not yet realized.
uncertainties: Credit split between theory (Zoller, Cirac, Jaksch) and experiment (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger) is unresolved.
Whether the simulation impact is lasting beyond the Mott demonstration is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED allows strong coupling of superconducting qubits to microwave resonators and dispersive readout, forming the architecture of most superconducting quantum processors. It is a clear, original and enormously influential concept with careful experimental demonstration.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal, and Wallraff with Schoelkopf and colleagues demonstrated strong coupling. Four credited names exceed the three-person limit; Blais is left out here. Overlap with the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits (Clarke, Devoret, Martinis) raises the question of recency.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature and independently reproduced, but a recent related prize may make the field feel recently recognized.
uncertainties: Excluding Blais from the three is a hard attribution choice.
Overlap with the recent superconducting-circuit prize may reduce timeliness.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade enables strongly interacting neutral atoms, and tweezer arrays now give programmable quantum simulators and gates of increasing fidelity. This is important and has moved fast from proposals to demonstrations.
assessment.attribution: Lukin and Jaksch proposed the blockade scheme; Saffman gave the gate proposals and experiments; Browaeys and Grangier did the early blockade experiments. With four credited names, choosing three means leaving out Grangier, and the credit line is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Maturity is moderate: the underlying blockade is well confirmed, but large-scale error-corrected computing and simulation are still developing, so recognition might be early.
uncertainties: Whether the full field has stabilized enough for a prize.
Allocation between early blockade experiments and later array platforms.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser, a bandgap-engineered unipolar mid-infrared source, made compact laser spectroscopy and trace-gas sensing possible across the molecular fingerprint region. For a spectroscopist this is a decisive enabling instrument with lasting application.
assessment.attribution: Faist, Capasso and colleagues (including Cho for molecular beam epitaxy growth) demonstrated the first device in 1994; Sirtori and Hutchinson also co-authored. The supplied trio is reasonable though Kazarinov and Suris proposed the concept in 1971 and could raise questions.
assessment.maturity: Mature, commercialized, and broadly used in spectroscopy and sensing for decades.
uncertainties: Role of Kazarinov and Suris and of other co-authors on the 1994 paper is not captured in the credit.
The prize might be seen as more an engineering invention than discovery of physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and demonstrating quantum control opened a measurement regime in which macroscopic objects are controlled and read at the quantum limit, with relevance to precision sensing and tests of quantum mechanics.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis (mechanical ground state, 2010), Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg (cavity optomechanics, sideband cooling) each made decisive contributions, and Painter and Regal/Lehnert also contributed. The supplied trio is arguable.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature; the central demonstrations are confirmed by several groups, but applications are still emerging and the foundations tests remain limited.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over many groups, and Martinis's role may clash with his recent prize.
Impact beyond sensing demonstrations is not yet settled.
